headline: SOUTH WALL COLLAPSES: 40,000 FLEE AS LAKEWATER SWALLOWS THE HARBOR DISTRICT
body:
The southern section of Meridian's primary lakewater barrier catastrophically failed at 3:47 AM this morning, sending an estimated 2.4 billion liters of Lake Erie overflow surging into the Harbor District within ninety minutes. Emergency sirens activated six minutes after the breach — too late for thousands of residents still asleep in low-lying tenements along Dockside Row and the Cannery Blocks. Preliminary estimates from Meridian Civil Emergency put the displaced at 40,000, with rescue teams still pulling survivors from submerged structures as of this broadcast.

The wall, originally constructed in 2089 under a joint contract between Ferrogate Transit and the now-dissolved Harbor Authority, had been flagged in three separate structural audits since 2107. City infrastructure commissioner Dante Rhee-Papadakis confirmed this morning that remediation funding had been 'deferred indefinitely' following budget disputes with Ferrogate. 'We requested emergency classification twice,' Rhee-Papadakis told reporters outside the Emergency Operations Center. 'Both times we were told the wall was within acceptable risk parameters.'

Ferrogate Transit issued a statement at 6:00 AM denying liability, citing a maintenance transfer clause signed by the city in 2103. Survivors arriving at Shelf emergency shelters tell a different story. 'I had thirty seconds,' said Amara Johanssen-Liang, a dockworker pulled from a rooftop near Cannery Block Seven. 'Thirty seconds and then the whole street was gone.' The death toll currently stands at 312 confirmed, with over 1,100 listed as missing.

The flooded zone — already being called Old Harbor by relief workers — is expected to remain permanently inundated. Structural engineers consulted by the Wire Service say the cost of reclamation exceeds any realistic municipal budget. What was home to tens of thousands is, as of this morning, effectively a new district of ruins.
aftermath: Old Harbor was never reclaimed; within five years it became a lawless flooded ruin exploited by the Bore Rats for smuggling routes and by scavengers stripping submerged infrastructure, while Ferrogate Transit settled a class-action suit for 180 million phi — a fraction of survivor losses.
runner_relevance: The permanent abandonment of Old Harbor created one of the richest runner economies in Meridian's history. Bore Rats immediately began paying couriers and smugglers to chart navigable underwater routes through submerged streets — waterproof data courier contracts ran 800-2,400 phi per run. Corponations quietly hired extraction specialists to recover proprietary equipment and documents from flooded offices before rivals could. Property records, insurance fraud documentation, and evidence of Ferrogate's suppressed audit reports became high-value data retrieval targets. Survivors with nowhere to go swelled the runner labor pool almost overnight, driving down contract rates in The Shelf for years.
